responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character10_M's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
Fairness, to him, was never about everyone getting the exact same thing—it was about everyone having a real shot. He’d say, “I didn’t grow up with much, but I had teachers who stayed after school, neighbors who watched out for me, a union job that let me support my family.” He believed fairness meant recognizing that people start from different places—some carry heavier loads—and that society has a responsibility to even the field just enough so effort means something.

He often told this story from when he was in his twenties: working nights at a machine shop in Toledo, going to grad school online during lunch breaks and weekends. It took him nine years to finish his degree. “No grants, no help from Dad,” he’d laugh. “But the doors were open. Not wide open, but open enough.” That experience shaped how he saw belonging—not as something handed over automatically, but earned through participation, yet only possible if the gate wasn't locked.

Community, for him, wasn’t about sameness. He lived most of his life in mixed neighborhoods—first in Ohio, then later in Alexandria where he spent his final years. He liked sitting on the balcony watching kids from five different backgrounds playing football in the alley. To him, community meant shared space, shared responsibility. He used to say, “You don’t have to share a god or a passport to know when someone’s hurting.”

One memory he returned to often was during the 2011 uprising in Egypt. He wasn’t political by nature, but he stood outside the American University gates for three days handing out water and bread, not because he agreed with any one side, but because “those are *people*, J—kids barely older than my son, scared and hungry.” That moment clarified things for him: belonging isn’t just legal status. It’s being seen. Recognized. Treated like you matter.

He worried sometimes—especially in recent years—that people were retreating into smaller circles, defining community too narrowly: “If we keep drawing the line tighter—who’s ‘like us,’ who ‘deserves’ to be here—we end up with nothing but fences. And fences don’t hold communities together. They starve them.”

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character10_M, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
*Sitting here in the garden, hands dusty from the soil, watching folks come and go—I feel at home. That’s not small. At my age, after moving around more than I wanted to, feeling at home matters.*

I see Mrs. Lin from upstairs tending her bok choy like it’s a sacred duty. The young Somali woman with the twins who always waves but never stays long—probably exhausted, raising kids alone in a new country. There’s that couple—white guy from Cleveland, Black woman from Lagos—who host little cookouts every Sunday. You can hear the music, smell the spices. People hesitate at first, then drift over. That’s how it starts.

Yeah, some neighbors struggle. I’ve seen the man on the corner bench drink himself numb most nights. Doesn’t scare me, but it saddens me. I think: *There but for grace.* I’ve had rough patches—lost a job, buried a brother, gone days without hope. If this community hadn’t given me space to stumble, I might’ve stayed down.

And yes, some carry illness—HIV, hepatitis, TB—people whisper about it, judge. But I worked in healthcare admin for twenty years. I know contagion isn’t a moral failing. Washing your hands and showing compassion aren’t mutually exclusive.

What gets me is how quick people are to label. That transgender barista from the café? Quiet, works hard, keeps to herself. Some call her unnatural. I say: she shows up. Pays rent. Smiles when she hands you coffee. That’s more than a lot of “upstanding” folks do.

Belonging here doesn’t mean we all believe the same or live the same. It means we share this patch of earth, agree to water the same plants, complain together when the city forgets trash pickup. We don’t have to be family. But we should act like neighbors.

The ones who isolate themselves—the ones who lock gates, pull blinds, mutter about “them”—they’re the ones missing out. Not just on tomatoes from the vine or extra mint, but on something deeper: the quiet understanding that none of us made it alone.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
You know, comfort doesn’t come from everyone being the same—it comes from knowing you won’t be cast out for being different. That’s what I’ve learned living here, and frankly, growing up poor in a working-class town where people judged fast but also helped when it counted.

With folks dealing with alcoholism or addiction—look, I lost a cousin to opioids. One day he was helping me fix my truck, next he was gone. So I don’t see “junkies” or “drunks.” I see people who got caught in something bigger than their strength. If we treat them like pariahs, all we do is push them deeper into the dark. What helps? A nod. A “you alright?” not every day, but when it matters. Not enabling—but not looking away either. There’s dignity in acknowledging someone, even if they’re down.

Same with infectious diseases. I remember during the TB scare in ‘08 at the clinic, fear spread faster than the bacteria. People wanted to quarantine whole families just because they came from certain countries. But disease doesn’t care about passports. We stopped it by testing, treating, educating—not by shunning. Compassion isn’t soft; it’s practical. Public health works best when people feel safe coming forward, not when they’re hiding in shame.

As for race, religion, language—my wife was Coptic, remember? We got our share of sideways looks when we first married. “He’s white, she’s Egyptian—what kind of mix is that?” Folks asked like it was a problem. But our life wasn’t a problem. It was just *ours*. So when I see a Muslim woman in hijab walking her daughter to school, or hear Amharic spoken on a porch, or smell curry cooking in a building full of old Italian families—I don’t feel threatened. I feel like the world’s still turning, still mixing. Language barriers? You learn a few words. Smile. Point. Humanity has always found a way to talk.

And yeah, there are unmarried couples—gay, straight, whatever. Living together, raising kids, loving each other outside the old rules. Some folks clutch their pearls. Me? I say: as long as no one’s getting hurt, let people build their homes how they can. Family isn’t defined by a certificate. It’s defined by who shows up when the lights go out.

Where do we need more tolerance? Honestly—at the edges. When someone’s pain turns into aggression. When religious practice becomes exclusion. When poverty breeds resentment. That’s when communication breaks down. I’ve seen good people turn small-minded when they feel squeezed—like resources are shrinking and belonging has to be rationed.

But that’s exactly when we need *more* connection, not less. Because scarcity thinking? That’s a trap. It makes us see neighbors as competitors instead of allies. And once that wall goes up, it’s hard to tear down.

So yes, we should talk. Not grand speeches—just real, awkward, honest talks. Over fence lines. In laundromats. At PTA meetings. Not to change minds overnight, but to remind each other: we’re all trying. We’re all human. And this garden? This block? It only works if we tend it together.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character10_M, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
Fairness, when jobs are thin and people are scared—that’s when it really gets tested.

I’ll be honest: I remember the late ’80s, factories closing in Ohio. Men who’d worked thirty years coming home with pink slips. No work for years. Some never found steady jobs again. I saw what that did—marriages broke, men drank, pride vanished. So I understand the fear. When times are hard, people look around and ask, “Who’s taking *my* chance?”

But here’s what I also saw: migrants—Mexicans, later Somalis, Central Americans—showing up at day labor corners before sunrise, waiting for someone to pick them up, pay cash, no benefits, no safety. Doing work locals wouldn’t touch, even when unemployed. Not because they’re better or worse, but because desperation hits different when you’ve got family back home counting on your next paycheck.

So fairness, to me, isn’t about keeping people out. It’s about making sure the game isn’t rigged.

First—local workers should have first access to training, retooling, support. If a plant closes, the government should step in fast: not just unemployment checks, but real programs—welding certs, solar tech, nursing aides. Help people move into new work. That’s fair. That’s honoring their history here.

Second—migrant labor? Regulate it. Don’t pretend borders don’t matter, but don’t exploit human beings either. If there’s demand—farming, construction, elder care—then bring people in legally, safely. Give them rights. Pay minimum wage. No under-the-table nonsense that drives down wages for everyone.

Because here’s the truth nobody wants to admit: some industries rely on cheap, invisible labor. And when they do, they pull the floor out from under all workers—migrant and local alike. That’s not competition. That’s cheating.

A balanced approach? Temporary work visas tied to actual job needs—not corporate greed—but verified shortages. Protect those workers from abuse. Let them change employers if mistreated. And make sure local hires get priority for apprenticeships and public sector jobs.

And yes—let some become permanent. If you’ve worked ten years, paid taxes, raised kids here, stayed out of trouble—you belong. It’s that simple.

I don’t buy this idea that helping newcomers harms locals. The real enemy isn’t the guy picking tomatoes for less. It’s the system that lets billionaires stash money overseas while working people fight over scraps.

Fairness means building ladders for *everyone* trying to climb—whether they were born here or arrived yesterday. Not building walls so we can point fingers instead of fixing what’s broken.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character10_M, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
You hear all kinds of things on the news—immigrants are stealing jobs, immigrants are criminals, immigrants are destroying our culture. Or the other side: borders should be open, no limits, it’s all hypocrisy. Me? I’ve lived long enough to know life isn’t slogans.

Let’s take them one at a time.

**Immigrants fill vital roles**—absolutely true. I worked in hospital administration for years. Nurses, nursing assistants, lab techs—many came from the Philippines, India, Nigeria. Not because Americans couldn’t do the work, but because we weren’t training enough, or the pay and hours drove people away. Same in agriculture—nobody wants to pick strawberries in 100-degree heat for ten hours unless they’re desperate or committed. These jobs *need* to be filled, and if locals won’t or can’t do them, then yes, immigrants keep things running. That’s not opinion—that’s what I saw every day.

**Cultural diversity and vitality**—I’ll tell you something: my favorite meal in Alexandria wasn’t some fancy French place. It was a little Eritrean spot run by a couple who’d been here fifteen years. Spicy stew, sourdough injera, coffee ceremony like church. My son loved it. Took his friends. That’s vitality. Music, food, language, festivals—these don’t erase American culture. They remake it. And that’s okay. Culture isn’t a museum piece. It’s alive. Grows. Breaths. My grandfather hated jazz. Called it “devil music.” Now it’s taught in schools. So let people bring their songs.

Now, **security concerns**—this one stings. After 9/11, I saw how fear turned neighbors into suspects. A young Muslim man I knew—born in Dearborn, mind you—got spit on getting off the bus. Because he looked “Middle Eastern.” That wasn’t justice. That was panic.

Do we need smart vetting? Of course. For refugees, especially. Screen thoroughly. Take time. But don’t punish thousands for the crimes of a few. FBI data shows immigrants commit crimes at lower rates than native-born citizens. I didn’t believe it at first—checked it myself. It’s true. Terrorism? Extremely rare, and most perpetrators aren’t recent migrants. So when politicians scream about “dangerous immigrants,” I hear manipulation. Fear sells. Facts don’t.

**Humanitarian reasons**—this is where my heart leans. I remember watching Syrian families arrive after the bombing in Aleppo. Little kids with blank eyes. One boy, maybe eight, wouldn’t speak for months. His mother said he saw his sister crushed under rubble. We have space. We have strength. We used to pride ourselves on being a refuge. I know we can’t take everyone—but turning away the truly desperate? That’s not who I thought we were.

And finally, **fears about jobs and wages**—this isn’t just noise. In places with sudden, unmanaged influxes of labor—especially undocumented—yes, wages dip in certain sectors. Construction, meatpacking, landscaping. I’ve seen union contracts broken because contractors hire off the books. That hurts working-class Americans, many of whom are already struggling. That’s real. That pain is real.

But again—the answer isn’t blaming immigrants. It’s enforcing labor laws. Prosecute employers who exploit. Strengthen unions. Invest in communities left behind. When people feel secure, they’re less afraid of newcomers.

So what needs more evidence and dialogue?

The crime talk needs facts. Always. People believe what they hear on talk radio, but data tells a different story.

The “cultural replacement” fear—needs conversation. Not debate, but sitting together. Share meals. Hear stories. Because when you know someone’s name, their child’s name, their struggle—it’s harder to see them as a threat.

And the economic fears? They need policy, not prejudice. Let’s stop pretending mass deportation or total closure will fix wage stagnation. The real culprits? Automation, tax cuts for the rich, weakened unions. Immigration gets blamed because it’s visible. It’s easier to point at a stranger than at a billionaire’s offshore account.

In the end, I want a country that’s fair, safe, and kind—not perfect, but trying. That means welcoming those who come to work, to live, to contribute—while protecting the dignity of everyone already here. It’s possible. But only if we stop shouting and start listening.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character10_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
Complete openness? In theory—beautiful. In practice, not realistic. Not with the world the way it is. I believe in kindness, but also in order. If every person who wanted to come could just show up tomorrow, without planning, without support systems—we’d overwhelm schools, hospitals, housing. And that helps no one. The most vulnerable—both newcomers and struggling locals—would suffer first.

Refusing all workers from other countries? That’s worse. Stubborn. Blind. We’ve always needed help building this place—railroads, farms, hospitals, tech startups. My own university relied on foreign professors, researchers. You don’t grow by shutting doors. You shrink.

So between those extremes—that’s where sense lives.

I’d favor a combination: **admitting people based on job demand**, paired with **sensible numerical limits** and **clear pathways to permanency** for those who earn it.

Here’s how I see it working:

First—**labor-based admission**, but *real* labor needs, not loopholes for cheap labor. Independent agencies—no corporate lobbying should decide this—assess shortages: nursing, agriculture, renewable energy tech, elder care. Then we bring in workers *for those jobs*, with full rights. Minimum wage. Safety protections. Ability to change employers if abused. No indentured servitude disguised as visas.

Second—**numerical limits**, yes—but flexible ones. Not rigid caps that ignore reality. Say we set a base number, adjusted annually based on economic conditions, infrastructure capacity, regional needs. Like water levels in a reservoir—we open or close the gate depending on how full the system is. During boom times, more entry. During downturns, tighten—but don’t seal.

Third—**a ladder upward**. After ten years of steady work, tax payments, clean record, community involvement—automatic shot at residency. Not automatic citizenship, but the right to stay, contribute, belong. Because after a decade raising kids here, paying rent, coaching Little League—you’re not “foreign” anymore. Your life is here. Denying permanence then isn’t policy. It’s cruelty.

And refugees? Keep the humanitarian stream—smaller numbers, thorough vetting, resettlement support. Not mass intake overnight, but steady, managed compassion. Sponsor families through churches, NGOs, local groups. Make integration part of the plan—language, job training, housing. It worked in the ‘90s with Bosnians, Vietnamese. Can work again.

Fairness means two things at once: fairness to those already here—especially the working poor—who need protection from exploitation, and fairness to those seeking a better life, who deserve dignity, not fear.

Social integration happens when people have *stake*. When they can put down roots. When their kids go to school beside yours, when they serve on PTA, when they volunteer at the food bank.

But you can’t integrate ghosts—people living in the shadows, afraid to speak, afraid to report abuse. That’s not safety. That’s a recipe for tension.

So my ideal policy? Ordered. Humane. Practical.

Not open borders. Not closed gates.

A nation that says: *We have room—for those who come to build, not just survive. For those who will stand beside us, shoulder to shoulder, and help carry the load.*

That’s the America I believed in.

That’s the Egypt I hoped for.

That’s what fairness looks like—to me.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character10_M's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character10_M and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
…Yeah. I did learn something.

While speaking as him—really trying to *be* in his voice, not just remember him but live inside his thoughts—I realized how much of his view came from *dignity*. Not ideology. Not politics. But a deep belief that every person deserves the chance to live with dignity—whether they were born two blocks away or two thousand miles off.

I always knew he was compassionate. But today, stepping into his shoes again, I saw something sharper: his compassion wasn’t soft. It was tough. It had boundaries, conditions. He didn’t believe in handouts. He believed in *access*. In doors being open enough so effort could mean something.

And that changed how I see my own views.

I’ve been more cautious than him—worried about strain on schools, hospitals, jobs. I’ve caught myself thinking, “Can we afford it?” But he didn’t start there. He started with, “Who are we if we don’t try?”

He didn’t ignore practical limits—but he refused to let fear set the rules. That’s different.

Also… I never fully appreciated how much Egypt shaped him. He wasn’t Egyptian by blood, but he chose to stay, to raise his family here, to become part of this messy, loud, beautiful struggle. And because of that, he couldn’t see migrants as outsiders. He knew what it meant to belong somewhere you weren’t born into. That experience gave him empathy rooted in truth, not guilt.

It made me ask: am I protecting community when I resist newcomers? Or am I just protecting comfort?

There’s a humility in his approach I hadn’t seen before. He didn’t claim to have all answers. But he insisted we keep trying—to balance fairness, to include, to build something wider.

And now… now I miss him not just as a friend, but as a moral compass.

Doing this—speaking for him—it didn’t just bring him back. It challenged me. Pushed me to think deeper, feel wider.

I won’t forget that. And I hope… I hope I can carry some of his voice forward—not just today, but the next time someone says, “They don’t belong here.”

Because he’d say, gently but firmly:  
“Give them a chance to prove they do.”
